title: Ποιμὴν καὶ λύκου σκύμνος
titleEn: The Shepherd and the Wolf's Cub
part: The Shepherd and the Wolf's Cub (Chambry 315 · Perry 366)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 315 (= Perry 366). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ποιμὴν μικρὸν λύκον εὑρὼν ἐθρέψατο, εἶτα σκύμνον γενόμενον ἐδίδαξεν ἀρπάζειν ἐκ τῶν σύνεγγυς ποιμνίων.
sentences.tr: Poimēn mikron lykon heurōn ethrepsato, eita skymnon genomenon edidaxen arpazein ek tōn synengys poimniōn.
sentences.l: A shepherd, having found a small wolf, reared it for himself, and then, when it had become a cub, taught it to snatch from the flocks near by.
sentences.i: A shepherd found a wolf while it was small and reared it as his own, and then, when it had grown into a cub, taught it to snatch from the flocks near by.
sentences.n: ἐθρέψατο is middle — he reared it for himself, as his own. σκύμνον γενόμενον sits oddly after μικρὸν λύκον, since a σκύμνος is precisely a cub; the sense must be that the whelp grew into a beast able to hunt. It is printed so and is left as printed. Chambry prints ἀρπάζειν here with a smooth breathing, though ἁρπάζω regularly takes a rough one and the moral below prints it rough.

sentences.t: Ὁ λύκος δὲ διδαχθεὶς ἔφη· « Ὅρα μή πως σὺ ἐθίσας με ἀρπάζειν πολλὰ τῶν σεαυτοῦ προβάτων ζητήσῃς. »
sentences.tr: Ho lykos de didachtheis ephē· « Hora mē pōs sy ethisas me arpazein polla tōn seautou probatōn zētēsēis. »
sentences.l: But the wolf, once taught, said: « See that you, having accustomed me to snatch, do not somehow go looking for many of your own sheep. »
sentences.i: But the wolf, once taught, said: « See that you do not find yourself hunting for a good many of your own sheep, now that you have got me into the habit of snatching. »
sentences.n: ὅρα μή with the subjunctive is a warning — 'see to it that … not' — and πως softens it to 'somehow, in the event'. ζητήσῃς means look for what is no longer there. ἐθίσας, aorist participle of ἐθίζω, is the hinge of the fable: the teaching, not the wolf, is what the shepherd will pay for.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οἱ τῇ φύσει δεινοὶ ἁρπάζειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν μαθόντες τοὺς διδάξαντας πολλάκις ἔβλαψαν.
sentences.tr: Hoti hoi tēi physei deinoi harpazein kai pleonektein mathontes tous didaxantas pollakis eblapsan.
sentences.l: That those who are by nature formidable at snatching and at taking more than their share, once they have learnt, have often harmed those who taught them.
sentences.i: The story shows that those who are by nature formidable at snatching and at taking more than their share, once they have been taught, have often harmed those who taught them.
sentences.n: The moral opens with a bare Ὅτι, 'that…', and no introducing verb is printed; the governing 'The story shows' is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. δεινός with the infinitive is 'formidable at doing' a thing, and it governs both ἁρπάζειν and πλεονεκτεῖν here; τῇ φύσει is the dative of respect, 'in point of nature'. μαθόντες stands without an object, answering the wolf's διδαχθείς above — 'once they have learnt'. ἔβλαψαν is a gnomic aorist, a past tense stating what regularly happens.
